item.title: Nvidia allegedly engineered scarcity by funding AI startups to buy its GPUs
item.description:
Source: www.techpowerup.com

Top Comment:

Reading this thread makes me realize that seemingly no one has heard the basic, mundane case for why Nvidia would want to do so much "circular financing" as a matter of totally normal business strategy. This may not be the whole story, but it's worth understanding.

Because of bottlenecks in the supply chain, Nvidia knows it is going to sell 100% of its inventory. They could raise prices quite a bit more, but then their only customers would be hyperscalers (building competing chips) and possibly OpenAI and Anthropic. Nvidia is willing to forgo present day profits for the strategic value of keeping its customer base diverse and promoting the network effects of e.g. CUDA. Instead of quoting a lower price per GPU to neoclouds and startups, they finance purchases of chips, but the two are roughly equivalent (financing means Nvidia takes on more risk, but has more upside and locks in future demand). It is in their commercial interest to have many competing buyers of their chips.

Obviously this creates fun mechanisms for fraud and wacky accounting (and I'm agnostic as to whether that's happening here), but it's worth knowing about the boring/obvious story before donning your tinfoil hat.

item.title: It Takes 16 Clicks for a Student to Open a PowerPoint on an iPad
item.description:
Source: www.reddit.com

Top Comment:

My employer (a large university) recently adopted a new parking portal. To pay for parking every morning, I have to open my browser, navigate to a webpage (there is no mobile app), and tap eleven times to pay for parking:

1. Tap "login", taking me to the login page.

2. Tap the "login" button on that page.

3. Sign in using 2FA. (A few more taps, but I'm not counting that against the portal).

4. Tap "Redeem Parking Permit"

5. Tap "Redeem use of Permit Pack"

6. Tap the car that I used that day (which is always the same car)

7. Tap "Confirm"

8. Tap the calendar icon to open the date chooser.

9. Tap on today's date (why isn't this the default?!)

10. Tap "Confirm"

11. Tap "Complete"

After a month or so at being annoyed by all of this unnecessary friction, I had Claude write an iOS app that keeps me logged into the parking portal. Now paying for parking requires just a single tap in my custom app. It also shows me a widget, telling me whether I have already paid or not.

I've built a lot with Claude this year, but that simple tool might be the one that brings me the most happiness.

item.title: Live airband on all frequencies from KORS. Victoria, CA also ground stopped
item.description:
Source: orcasairband.com

Top Comment:

Hi all. Thanks for the interest. I'm going to post an impromptu blog post here just explaining what this is. The rather unfortunate ground stop today made this unexpectedly useful with the pilots here on Orcas just to get a sense of the chatter in our airspace re the situation.

This is an ETTUS B210 attached to a dual 4090 box. It's a polyphase channelizer that takes the entire airband, channelizes it using cuda code on GPU, demodulates it, detects transmissions, throws away data tx and then feeds the tx through a voice model I created for transcription. A separate LLM reads the transcriptions to create a situational awareness picture of the airspace.

I'm interested in open sourcing this and making it available for folks who can run an ETTUS B210 or high quality SDR with enoguh bandwidth and a local GPU machine, so that we can cover more airpsace.

This was born out of an incident we had not too long ago where a pilot around KORS (based at Friday Harbor) lost the engine in his 172, and put it in the water in front of a ferry and was picked up by the ferry. We're a pretty close bunch on Orcas Island and we only heard about it days later via social media. That felt completely unacceptable, and I set out to create a radio that could monitor everything in real-time, all the time, and alert on emergencies. That has extended to transcribing and creating situational awareness for a chunk of airspace.

I'm an IFR pilot. I fly a T206H regularly in IMC around here and I'm a ground instructor. You can email me at mark@defiant.com or find me on x at mmaunder if you'd like to connect. I'm particularly interested in hearing from folks who can run a station on their own hardware and are under bravo or a charlie or even just somewhere interesting re airspace.

item.title: After 600 experiments, here's what I discovered about JEPA world models
item.description:
Source: haddyalchaer.com

Top Comment:

There’s a repeated theme here that I don’t understand. For example:

> (3) That's where I decided to build a harder test, where each task takes its start from one demonstration and its goal from another

> (4) I also built an interactive demo where I could place the block anywhere and pick any goal. [but] The goals in the harder test are frames from expert demonstrations

Why lean so hard on the demonstration examples? Surely the actual task here is to move between any two arbitrary poses.

So if the demonstration set is statistically strange in any way, you keep banging into that. And even if you get great results, you still haven’t shown that it generalizes to the generic system. And the one thing you know 100% about a physical robot system is that you will never encounter exactly the same situation twice.

Is there actually a reason to pick eval examples from the demonstrations instead of independent samples from the underlying task?

I’m pretty sure that the T-shoving problem doesn’t have goal reachability issues. And if it did, test 4 could run into them since the start pose is arbitrary.

item.title: Show HN: Isometric SF – A pixel-art map of the SF Bay Area
item.description:
Source: isometricsf.com

Technical Write-up: https://www.justinchavez.com/blog/isometric-sf-how/

Hi HN! Showcasing this fun project. I took 1300 square miles of the SF Bay Area from Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles and transformed them into a cohesive pixel map. It's really fun to explore and stumble upon various famous landmarks like Apple Park, Palace of Fine Arts, or UC Berkeley.

The technicals involve using Nano Banana 2 to train a Qwen-Image-Edit 2511 LoRA which is used to prototype the style and generation methods. For final map I used Qwen to train a Klein 4B LoRA which reproduced the style at 1/4 of the cost. More details in the blog post.

Let me know what you think! I really enjoyed this process of fine-tuning smaller open source models.

If I did the map with Nano Banana 2 it would have cost around 7k USD!

Credit for the idea goes to Isometric NYC.
